common_name: Ice N' Roses White Hellebore (Gold Collection Sterile Pure-White Snow Rose)
scientific_name: Helleborus x glandorfensis 'HGC Ice N' Roses White'

planting.note: Transplant container-grown plants in fall or early spring into rich, sharply drained soil in partial shade; Ice N' Roses White is a sterile Gold Collection hybrid bred in Germany by Josef Heuger, crossing Helleborus x ericsmithii with H. x hybridus.

directions: Site in humus-rich soil with reliably sharp drainage, in partial to light shade; soggy winter ground is the most common cause of failure. Ice N' Roses White carries clusters of large, outward-facing, pure white flowers that age to soft green as they mature, held on sturdy stems above glossy, leathery evergreen foliage from late winter into spring. Being a sterile Gold Collection cross, it never diverts energy into abundant self-sown seedlings the way ordinary Lenten rose does, so clumps stay tidy and the named color holds true for the life of the plant. Shear away tattered old leaves in late winter just before the flower stalks rise to best display the bloom.

common_name: Ice N' Roses Rose Hellebore (Gold Collection Sterile Rose-Pink Snow Rose)
scientific_name: Helleborus x glandorfensis 'HGC Ice N' Roses Rose'

planting.note: Transplant container-grown plants in fall or early spring into rich, sharply drained soil in partial shade; Ice N' Roses Rose is a sterile Gold Collection hybrid bred in Germany by Josef Heuger, crossing Helleborus x ericsmithii with H. x hybridus.

directions: Grow in rich, evenly moist but sharply drained soil in partial to light shade, improving heavy clay with compost before planting. Ice N' Roses Rose opens rounded, outward-facing flowers in a clear rose-pink that deepens slightly with age, set against dark, glossy, leathery foliage held in a neat mound through winter. As with its Gold Collection siblings the cross is sterile, so the plant channels its energy into a long-lived, well-behaved clump rather than seedlings, and the flower color stays consistent year after year. Cut tired old leaves back in late winter just before bud break to let the flowers take center stage.

planting.note: Plant in fall or early spring in rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Masquerade is part of the Winter Jewels breeding series, selected for frilled, heavily picoteed double flowers blooming in late winter to early spring.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and keep the root zone evenly moist as the clump establishes. Masquerade is one of the named selections within the Winter Jewels hellebore strain, bearing frilled, fully double flowers in cream to pale pink with a bold dark picotee edge on each petal, carried above deeply divided, leathery evergreen leaves. Flowering begins in the depths of winter and continues into early spring, often overlapping with the last snow, and the sturdy nodding blooms hold up well to late cold snaps. Remove old, weather-worn foliage in late winter just before flowering so the intricate blooms are fully visible, and keep the toxic foliage and roots away from areas where children or pets forage.
sources: Northwest Garden Nursery — Winter Jewels hellebore breeding

planting.note: Transplant container-grown plants in fall or early spring into rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Walberton's Rosemary was raised by David Tristram at Walberton Nursery in the UK and is one of the most widely distributed patented Lenten rose selections sold through garden centers.

directions: Plant in rich, humus-laden soil with good drainage, in partial to full shade; established clumps tolerate drier summer shade better than most perennials. Walberton's Rosemary produces an abundance of outward-facing, soft rose-pink single flowers with a faint darker veining, carried well above the handsome dark green, leathery foliage over a long late-winter-to-spring season. It is valued commercially for its free-flowering habit and compact, uniform growth compared with unselected Lenten rose seedlings, making it a reliable choice for mixed shade borders and containers alike. Tidy the clump by removing old leaves in late winter just before the new flower stalks emerge, and divide only when clumps become crowded, since hellebores otherwise resent disturbance.

planting.note: Plant dormant crowns in fall into gritty, fast-draining soil in part shade; this unusual species from southeastern Turkey and northern Syria goes fully dormant and leafless through summer heat, unlike the evergreen garden hellebores.

directions: Give the bladder hellebore gritty, sharply drained soil in part shade, ideally at the base of a rock or wall that sheds summer rain, since it is adapted to dry, baking summers in its native limestone hills. Pale green, deeply lobed leaves and unusual maroon-flushed, inflated bell-shaped flowers appear together in late winter, followed by distinctive papery, balloon-like seed pods that give the species its common name. The plant dies back completely and goes dormant through summer heat, so mark its location and withhold water once foliage yellows to avoid rotting the resting rootstock. It is a specialist's plant best suited to rock gardens, raised beds, or alpine house culture rather than a typical moist shade border.
